deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page treats li/Ei, i.e. \int e^x dx/x, and its divergent expansion 1 - 1/x + 2/x^2 - .... On this page Riemann (i) evaluates Ei(10) numerically from the divergent asymptotic series, (ii) studies the integral that gives the remainder after optimal truncation, (iii) evaluates that integral by a saddle-point (steepest-descent) expansion about x=m, and (iv) records Stirling's series.

(1) Numerical evaluation. Riemann writes Ei(x) ~ e^x (1/x + 1/x^2 + 1!·2/x^3 + 3!/x^4 + ...) and puts x=10. The terms k!/10^{k+1} for k=0..9 are 0.1, 0.01, 0.002, 0.0006, 0.00024, 0.00012, 0.000072, 0.0000504, 0.00004032, 0.000036288. He stops where the terms stop decreasing (9!/10^10 = 10!/10^11), which is optimal truncation. Their sum is 0.113159008.
- He multiplies by e^10 = 22026.5 using base-10 logarithms: log10(0.113159008) = 9.053690 - 10 and log10(e^10) = 4.342945.
- The sum is (1)3.396635, so Ei(10) ≈ 10^3.396635 ≈ 2492.5. The true value is 2492.23.
- He then starts the same for x=5: 1/5 = 0.2, 1/25 = 0.04, 2/125 = 0.016, 6/625 = 0.0096, 24/3125 = 0.00768.

(2) The remainder integral. The tail after the term (m-2)!/x^{m-1} is (m-1)! \int e^x x^{-m} dx (title: '(m-1)! \int e^x dx/x^m'). He tries Euler's integral (m-1)! = \int_0^\infty e^{-s}s^{m-1}ds to rewrite x^{-m}. This gives double integrals such as \int_m^\infty e^x dx \int_0^\infty e^{-s/x}s^{m-1}ds and, after x = m·x, m\int_1^\infty e^{mx}dx\int e^{-s/(xm)}s^{m-1}ds. The struck-out Bessel-type forms \int\int e^{s(x-1/x)}s^{2m-1} and the completed square e^{(\sqrt x + 2si/\sqrt x)^2} belong to the same attempt, which he abandons.

(3) Saddle point. He writes the integrand as e^{x - m log x}. The derivative 1 - m/x vanishes at x=m, where the exponent is m - m log m. With x = m(1+t) [the page writes x/m = t; the shift is mine] one gets
x - m log x = m - m log m + m(t - log(1+t)),
t - log(1+t) = t^2/2 - t^3/3 + t^4/4 - t^5/5 + ....
Hence \int e^x x^{-m}dx = e^m m^{-m}·m\int e^{m(t^2/2 - t^3/3 + t^4/4 - ...)}dt. The page writes the prefactor as 'e^{-m}'; this is a slip.
- He separates the Gaussian factor e^{m t^2/2} and expands the rest: 1 + m t^3(-1/3 + t/4 - t^2/5) + (m^2/2) t^6(-1/3 + t/4 - ...)^2.
- He also writes the remainder as \int e^{m t^2/2}·(e^{m(t - t^2/2 - log(1+t))} - 1)/t · t dt and integrates by parts, using d/dt(t - log(1+t)) = t/(1+t).
- Along the real axis x=m is a minimum, so the steepest path is vertical. With t = iu, \int e^{-u^2}du = \sqrt\pi/2 gives the leading term i\sqrt{2\pi}·e^m m^{-m} m^{1/2}, exactly as on the page.
- This equals the leading asymptotic of 2\pi i/\Gamma(m), i.e. Hankel's loop integral for 1/\Gamma evaluated by steepest descent.
- Collecting terms through order 1/m gives m + (1/3)m^2 t^3 + m^2 t^4/4 - (1/18)m^3 t^6. The signs fit the rotated variable u (t^4 → u^4, t^6 → -u^6).
- Over the full line the odd term drops out. With <u^4> = 3/m^2 and <u^6> = 15/m^3 the even terms give the relative correction 3/(4m) - 15/(18m) = -1/(12m), consistent with 1/\Gamma.

(4) Stirling's series. As a check he writes log\Pi(m-1) = log\Gamma(m) = (m-1/2)log m - m + (1/2)log 2\pi + 1/(12m) - 1/(360m^3) + 1/(42·5·6·m^5), with 42·5·6 = 1260.

(5) Half-range integral. Last line: \int_0^\infty e^{-y/2} y dy·(1/3)·(1/2) = 2/3 [the bookkeeping is my interpretation]. This is the odd term m^2 t^3/3 integrated over a half-line with y = m t^2 (\int_0^\infty e^{-y/2}y dy = 4, divided by 6). It gives the real contribution (2/3)e^m m^{-m} of the integral starting at the saddle point.
- Multiplying by (m-1)! ≈ \sqrt{2\pi} m^{m-1/2}e^{-m} gives '(2/3) m^{-1/2}\sqrt{2\pi}', the second expression on the last line.
- Interpretation (mine, strongly supported numerically): when the series for e^{-x}Ei(x) is truncated near its smallest term (m = x), the remainder is about 2/3 of the first omitted term (2/3)(m-1)!/m^m. Equivalently it is ≈ (2/3)\sqrt{2\pi/m}e^{-m} relative to e^m.
- Check at x=10, m=10: the sum of the 9 terms k=0..8 is 0.11312272. The true value is e^{-10}Ei(10) = 0.1131473. The difference is 2.46e-5 ≈ 0.68 × 9!/10^10, against the predicted 2/3.
- So Riemann is computing the 'converging factor' of the divergent Ei/li series at optimal truncation by a saddle-point analysis.
errors: Prefactor slip: the page writes e^{-m}\int e^{m(t-log(1+t))} m dt for the integral of e^x x^{-m}. The correct substitution gives e^{m} m^{-m}·m\int e^{m(t-log(1+t))}dt.
Gamma substitution slip: \int_0^\infty e^{-s/x}s^{m-1}ds = (m-1)! x^{m}, not (m-1)! x^{-m}. Representing x^{-m} needs e^{-sx}. The double-integral attempt is in any case abandoned.

Signs of the Gaussian exponent (e^{+m t^2/2}) are left formal. They make sense only after rotating to the vertical steepest-descent path t = iu, which the factor i in the result shows Riemann intended. The final correction line is consistent with the rotated variable.

Numerics: e^{10}×0.113159008 ≈ 2492.5 versus the true Ei(10) = 2492.23. This discrepancy is inherent to the truncated divergent series, not an arithmetic error. The logarithms 9.053690, 4.342945 and 3.396635 are correct.
The digit placement of the small terms (0,000072, 0,0000504, 0,00004032, 0,000036288) is correct on the page but garbled in the transcription.

results.what: Numerical evaluation of Ei(10) (hence li(e^10)) from the divergent series e^x Σ k!/x^{k+1}, truncated at the smallest term; sum 0.113159008, value ≈ 2492.5
results.modern_name: Optimal truncation of an asymptotic series (superasymptotics)
results.usually_credited_to: Practice goes back to Euler/Legendre/Gauss; systematic theory to Stieltjes (1886), Dingle, Berry

results.what: Expansion about the saddle x=m of e^{x - m log x}, x = m(1+t), t - log(1+t) = t^2/2 - t^3/3 + ...; vertical steepest path giving \int e^x x^{-m}dx ≈ i\sqrt{2\pi} e^m m^{1/2-m} (= 2\pi i/\Gamma(m))
results.modern_name: Saddle-point / steepest-descent asymptotics of Hankel's integral for 1/Gamma
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace (real case); Riemann 1863 fragment on hypergeometric series; Debye 1909

results.what: First correction from Gaussian moments (m u^4/4 - m^2 u^6/18 → ∓1/(12m))
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace; Stirling/de Moivre for the series

results.what: Stirling series for log Γ(m) through 1/(1260 m^5)

Half-range saddle integral: odd cubic term gives 2/3 e^m m^{-m}; times (m-1)! gives (2/3)\sqrt{2\pi/m}. I.e. the remainder of the Ei/li series at optimal truncation is ≈ 2/3 of the first omitted term (numerically confirmed at x=10)
results.modern_name: Converging factor / terminant of the exponential-integral asymptotic series (cf. Ramanujan's 1/3 in Γ(n,n), Airey 1937, Dingle, Berry 1989)
results.usually_credited_to: Stieltjes 1886 (alternating case), Airey 1937, Dingle 1973, Berry; the analogous constant 1/3 to Ramanujan (1911) and Szegő/Watson (1928-9)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's use of steepest descent is already known from his 1863 hypergeometric fragment, and Stirling's series is routine. What is notable is applying a saddle-point analysis to the remainder of the divergent li/Ei series at optimal truncation, obtaining the 2/3 converging factor (≈ Ramanujan-type 1/3 constant). That is an unpublished detail anticipating later converging-factor/terminant work. The reading rests on interpretation of terse notes, though the numerical agreement (0.68 vs 2/3) is strong.

transcription_corrections: The terms at x=10 should read 0,000072; 0,0000504; 0,00004032; 0,000036288 (the transcription shifts decimals). The sum line reads 0,113159008, not '0,1131,59008'.
'e^{10} = 22026,5' (the comma is misplaced in the image/transcription); the logarithm column is 9,053690 + 4,342945 = (1)3,396635.
'1 - \partial m/\partial x' is better read as 1 - m/x (derivative of x - m log x).
The final line is best read as \int_0^\infty e^{-y/2} y dy ·(1/3)·(1/2) → 2/3 · e^m m^{-m}, followed by (2/3) m^{-1/2}\sqrt{2\pi}.
'42·5·6·m^5' = 1260 m^5 in the Stirling series (the transcription has this correctly).
